D. Growth and Development Accounting

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code

Learning goals

Two simple questions sit behind much of growth economics. Why did an economy grow as fast as it did? And why is one economy so much richer than another? Growth accounting answers the first question, and development accounting answers the second. Both split output into a part explained by measured inputs (physical capital, workers, hours, schooling) and a part that is left over, total factor productivity (TFP). This appendix applies both methods to the Penn World Table, for any economies you choose. By the end of it you will be able to:

  • explain what the Penn World Table is, find the variables that the two methods need, and load them in Python, both from the official file and from the book’s prepared file;
  • derive the growth accounting equation from a Cobb–Douglas production function, and compute the contributions of capital, labour and TFP to GDP growth for every year since 1990;
  • derive the development accounting equation in its capital–output form, and split each economy’s income gap with the United States into TFP, physical capital and human capital;
  • measure how much of the differences in income across countries the inputs can explain, with the “success” measure of development accounting;
  • test how the answers change with the capital share, the measure of labour, country labour shares and natural-resource rents;
  • write short pandas functions (groupby, pct_change, merge, melt) and draw interactive Plotly charts that update when you choose other countries.

The appendix builds on the production model of Chapter 4, which does a first development accounting exercise with physical capital only, and on the growth accounting of Chapter 6, which uses U.S. data. The growth rules it uses are reviewed in Appendix C.5.

The growth accounting of Sections D.4 to D.7 follows the method of the Growth Atlas, a study companion built on Penn World Table 11.0. The development accounting of Sections D.8 to D.11 follows the code of Julieta Caunedo’s STEG lecture on income accounting, which we translate from Stata to Python.

D.1 Two questions, two methods

Both methods start from the same production function, the one of Chapters 4 to 6:

\[ Y = A K^{\alpha} L^{1-\alpha}, \qquad 0 < \alpha < 1. \tag{1} \]

Output \(Y\) is made with physical capital \(K\) and labour \(L\), and \(A\) is total factor productivity: how efficiently the economy turns its inputs into output. The exponent \(\alpha\) is the capital share. We can measure \(Y\), \(K\) and \(L\) in national data, but not \(A\). Both methods therefore find \(A\) the same way: as the part of output that the measured inputs do not explain, the residual.

Growth accounting Development accounting
Question Why did this economy grow? Why is this economy poorer than the United States?
Compares one economy with itself, year after year many economies with each other, in one year
Works with growth rates of total GDP, capital and labour levels of output per worker, capital and schooling
Main result contributions of capital, labour and TFP to GDP growth, in percentage points the share of the income gap due to TFP, physical capital and human capital
Sections D.4 to D.7 D.8 to D.11

Both methods are accounting, not explanation. They tell us where growth and income differences appear in equation (1), not why an economy invested more, schooled its workers longer, or used its inputs more efficiently. The models of Chapters 5 and 6 answer those questions.

Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

Choose your countries

Every chart of this appendix is drawn for a list of economies that you choose. Economies are named by their three-letter ISO code: USA for the United States, MEX for Mexico, CHN for China, IND for India, KOR for South Korea and NGA for Nigeria. To use other economies, change the list below and choose Runtime → Run all again. Section D.3 prints the codes of all 185 economies. In Colab, each chart also has a menu where you can pick economies with the mouse (hold Ctrl, or ⌘ on a Mac, to pick several).

COUNTRIES = ["USA", "MEX", "CHN", "IND", "KOR", "NGA"]   # your economies: change them!
ALPHA = 0.33                                             # the capital share, alpha
START, END = 1990, 2023                                  # the years of the growth accounting

Python note. Names in capital letters, such as COUNTRIES or ALPHA, are constants: values we set once at the top and use everywhere below. Changing them in one place changes the whole analysis.

D.3 The Penn World Table

The Penn World Table (PWT) is a database of national accounts for 185 economies since 1950, built at the Groningen Growth and Development Centre of the University of Groningen (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015). It is the standard source for growth and development accounting, for two reasons:

  • it makes output comparable across countries: GDP is converted with purchasing power parities (PPPs), so a dollar buys the same basket of goods everywhere, as Chapter 3 explains;
  • it provides the inputs of the production function: capital stocks built from past investment, the number of workers, their hours, and an index of their schooling.

We use version 11.0, released in 2025, which covers 1950 to 2023 with prices of 2021. These are the variables we need:

Variable What it measures Unit Used in
rgdpna real GDP at constant national prices million 2021 US$ growth accounting
rnna capital stock at constant national prices million 2021 US$ growth accounting
emp persons engaged (workers) millions both
avh average hours worked per worker in a year hours both
hc human capital index, from years of schooling and the return to schooling index both
rgdpo real GDP at chained PPPs, output side million 2021 US$ development accounting
cgdpo GDP at current PPPs, output side million 2021 US$ development accounting
cn capital stock at current PPPs million 2021 US$ development accounting
labsh share of labour income in GDP share Section D.11

Why two kinds of GDP? PWT recommends the national-price series (rgdpna, rnna) to compare growth rates over time within one economy, and the PPP series (rgdpo, cgdpo, cn) to compare levels across economies in one year. Growth accounting needs the first kind, development accounting the second.

Download the official file

The official data are a Stata file, pwt110.dta (about 4 MB), on the DataverseNL repository. pandas reads it straight from the web with pd.read_stata. The cell below downloads it, keeps the economies and years of this appendix, and prints its size.

    print("Official PWT 11.0:", official.shape[0], "rows and", official.shape[1], "columns")
    print("Years:", official["year"].min(), "to", official["year"].max())
except Exception as error:

Python note. groupby("year")[...].count() counts the non-missing values of each column, year by year. melt turns the six count columns into two columns, variable and economies, the “long” shape that Plotly Express wants: one row per point, and one column that names the line.

What to notice.

  • GDP, capital and the number of workers exist for about 180 economies since 2000.
  • Human capital (hc) is missing for about 40 economies, mostly small islands and oil states.
  • Hours worked (avh) cover only about 50 economies before 1990, mostly rich ones, and 130 since 2010. This is why the Growth Atlas, and Sections D.5 to D.9, measure labour by persons engaged by default, with hours as an option.

dropna removes the years with no hours, and groupby(...).min() finds the first year left for each country. All six default countries have hours in 2023, but Nigeria’s start only in 2005. With labour measured in hours, its growth accounting therefore starts in 2006.

Fig. 2: A first look at your countries

Goal. Compare output per worker in your countries over time. Output per worker is the quantity that development accounting explains in Section D.9.

We compute it as PPP output (rgdpo) divided by persons engaged (emp). Both are in millions, so the ratio is in dollars per worker. A ratio scale shows equal growth rates as equal slopes (Appendix C).

pwt["y_worker"] = pwt["rgdpo"] / pwt["emp"]      # output per worker, 2021 US$ at PPP

def country_picker(value):
    """A menu of all economies, by name, that returns their codes."""
    options = sorted((name, code) for code, name in NAMES.items())
    return SelectMultiple(options=options, value=tuple(value), rows=8, description="economies", style=WIDE)

PALETTE = [BLUE, RUST, GREEN, PURPLE, TEAL, "#d4a017", "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47", "#c2185b", "#6d4c41",
           "#00897b", "#7cb342", "#5e35b1", "#f4511e", "#3949ab", GRAY]

def country_colors(codes):
    """One fixed colour per economy: COUNTRIES first, in order, then the next free colours."""
    colors = {}
    order = list(COUNTRIES)
    for code in codes:
        if code not in order:
            order.append(code)
    for i, code in enumerate(order):
        colors[NAMES[code]] = PALETTE[i % len(PALETTE)]
    return colors

Python note. country_colors returns a dictionary from country names to colours. Passing it to Plotly Express as color_discrete_map keeps each economy’s colour when you add or remove others in the menu.

def output_figure(codes=tuple(COUNTRIES)):
    """Fig. 2: output per worker for the chosen economies, ratio scale."""
    chosen = pwt[pwt["iso3"].isin(codes)]
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="y_worker", color="country", log_y=True,
                  color_discrete_map=country_colors(codes),
                  range_x=[1970, 2023], range_y=[500, 400000],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "y_worker": "Output per worker (2021 US$ at PPP, ratio scale)",
                          "country": ""},
                  title=f"Output per worker since 1970: {len(codes)} economies")
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000, 300000])
    return fig

output_figure()

What to notice. Since 1970, China’s output per worker rose about 27-fold and Korea’s about 12-fold, while the U.S. level about doubled. Mexico’s output per worker was lower in 2023 than in 1980, and Nigeria’s is less than a tenth of the U.S. level. Large and lasting gaps like these are what development accounting tries to explain.

D.4 Growth accounting: the theory

Assumptions

  1. Output is produced with the Cobb–Douglas production function (1), \(Y_t = A_t K_t^{\alpha} L_t^{1-\alpha}\), in every year \(t\).
  2. The capital share \(\alpha\) is the same in every economy and every year. Following the Growth Atlas and Hall and Jones (1999), we use \(\alpha = 0.33\), about one third.
  3. Output \(Y_t\) is real GDP (rgdpna), capital \(K_t\) is the real capital stock (rnna), and labour \(L_t\) is one of three measures: persons engaged (emp), total hours (emp × avh), or quality-adjusted hours (emp × avh × hc).

Deriving the equation

Take natural logs of equation (1). The log of a product is the sum of the logs, and the log of a power is the exponent times the log:

\[ \ln Y_t = \ln A_t + \alpha \ln K_t + (1-\alpha) \ln L_t . \]

The same equation holds a year earlier, at \(t-1\). Subtract the two:

\[ \ln Y_t - \ln Y_{t-1} = (\ln A_t - \ln A_{t-1}) + \alpha (\ln K_t - \ln K_{t-1}) + (1-\alpha)(\ln L_t - \ln L_{t-1}). \]

The change in the log of a variable is, approximately, its growth rate: \(\ln X_t - \ln X_{t-1} \approx \Delta X / X\). Writing \(g_X\) for the growth rate of \(X\) gives the growth accounting equation:

\[ g_Y = \underbrace{\alpha\, g_K}_{\text{capital}} + \underbrace{(1-\alpha)\, g_L}_{\text{labour}} + \underbrace{g_A}_{\text{TFP}} . \tag{2} \]

GDP growth is the sum of three contributions: the growth of capital weighted by its share \(\alpha\), the growth of labour weighted by its share \(1-\alpha\), and the growth of TFP.

The residual

We observe \(g_Y\), \(g_K\) and \(g_L\), but not \(g_A\). So we turn equation (2) around:

\[ g_A = g_Y - \alpha\, g_K - (1-\alpha)\, g_L . \tag{3} \]

TFP growth is whatever GDP growth the inputs cannot explain: the Solow residual. Because it is computed this way, the three contributions always add up to GDP growth exactly, even though equation (2) holds only approximately for growth rates. Like the Growth Atlas, we use simple yearly growth rates, \(g_X = 100 \times (X_t / X_{t-1} - 1)\), in percent, so each contribution is in percentage points.

Intuition. With \(\alpha = 0.33\), a 3 percent rise in the capital stock adds about 1 percentage point to GDP growth, and a 3 percent rise in labour adds about 2 points. Whatever growth is left is credited to TFP.

What the residual contains. Over long periods, TFP growth reflects new ideas (Chapter 6), better organization, and the movement of workers to more productive jobs. In a single year it also absorbs anything the inputs miss: changes in hours or skills when labour is counted in persons, how intensively machines are used in booms and recessions, commodity price swings, wars, and measurement error. Treat a large residual in a single year with care.

D.5 Growth accounting for one economy, step by step

Goal. Compute equation (3) by hand for the United States, one column at a time, and check that the contributions add up.

Step 1: the labour input. We start with persons engaged, the Growth Atlas default.

us = pwt[pwt["iso3"] == "USA"][["year", "rgdpna", "rnna", "emp"]].copy()
us["L"] = us["emp"]
us.tail(3)
year rgdpna rnna emp L
9061 2021 23681000.0 78159000.0 160.86 160.86
9062 2022 24276000.0 79490000.0 165.58 165.58
9063 2023 24977000.0 80823000.0 167.54 167.54

Step 2: growth rates. pct_change() computes \(X_t / X_{t-1} - 1\) for every row of a column.

us["g_Y"] = us["rgdpna"].pct_change() * 100
us["g_K"] = us["rnna"].pct_change() * 100
us["g_L"] = us["L"].pct_change() * 100
us[["year", "g_Y", "g_K", "g_L"]].tail(3).round(2)
year g_Y g_K g_L
9061 2021 6.05 1.79 3.82
9062 2022 2.51 1.70 2.93
9063 2023 2.89 1.68 1.18

Step 3: the contributions, equations (2) and (3).

us["capital"] = ALPHA * us["g_K"]
us["labour"] = (1 - ALPHA) * us["g_L"]
us["tfp"] = us["g_Y"] - us["capital"] - us["labour"]

These numbers match the Growth Atlas, which publishes the same decomposition. For example, the Atlas reports U.S. GDP growth of 2.89 percent in 2023, with contributions of 0.55 (capital), 0.79 (labour) and 1.54 (TFP) percentage points.

A function for any economy and any labour measure

Steps 1 to 3 become one function. It works on many economies at once: groupby("iso3") makes pct_change compute growth rates within each economy, so the first year of one economy is never compared with the last year of another.

LABOUR = {"persons": "Persons engaged", "hours": "Total hours", "quality": "Quality-adjusted hours"}
LABOUR_MENU = [("Persons engaged", "persons"), ("Total hours", "hours"), ("Quality-adjusted hours", "quality")]

def growth_accounting(alpha=ALPHA, labour="persons"):
    """Equations (2) and (3) for every economy: contributions to GDP growth, in percentage points."""
    d = pwt.sort_values(["iso3", "year"]).copy()
    d["L"] = d["emp"]
    if labour in ("hours", "quality"):
        d["L"] = d["L"] * d["avh"]
    if labour == "quality":
        d["L"] = d["L"] * d["hc"]
    growth = d.groupby("iso3")[["rgdpna", "rnna", "L"]].pct_change(fill_method=None) * 100
    d["gdp"] = growth["rgdpna"]
    d["capital"] = alpha * growth["rnna"]
    d["labour"] = (1 - alpha) * growth["L"]
    d["tfp"] = d["gdp"] - d["capital"] - d["labour"]
    d = d[(d["year"] >= START) & (d["year"] <= END)]
    return d[["iso3", "country", "year", "gdp", "capital", "labour", "tfp"]].dropna()

ga = growth_accounting()
print(ga["iso3"].nunique(), "economies,", len(ga), "economy-years")
ga[ga["iso3"].isin(COUNTRIES)].groupby("country")[["gdp", "capital", "labour", "tfp"]].mean().round(2)

Python note. pct_change(fill_method=None) leaves a growth rate missing when either year is missing, instead of filling the gap. dropna() then removes the rows with any missing value.

Fig. 3: The growth accounting of one economy

Goal. Draw the decomposition year by year: stacked bars for the three contributions, and a line for GDP growth. The bars of each year add up to the line.

PARTS = [("capital", "Capital, αg_K", BLUE), ("labour", "Labour, (1−α)g_L", GREEN), ("tfp", "TFP, g_A", RUST)]

def add_decomposition(fig, d, row=None, col=None, legend=True):
    """Add the three contribution bars and the GDP growth line of one economy to a figure."""
    for column, label, color in PARTS:
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=d["year"], y=d[column], name=label, marker_color=color,
                             legendgroup=column, showlegend=legend), row=row, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=d["year"], y=d["gdp"], mode="lines+markers", name="GDP growth, g_Y",
                             line=dict(color="black", width=2), marker=dict(size=4),
                             legendgroup="gdp", showlegend=legend), row=row, col=col)
    return fig

def decomposition_figure(code="USA", alpha=ALPHA, labour="persons"):
    """Fig. 3: contributions to GDP growth in one economy, equation (2)."""
    d = growth_accounting(alpha, labour)
    d = d[d["iso3"] == code]
    fig = add_decomposition(go.Figure(), d)
    fig.update_layout(barmode="relative", title=f"{NAMES[code]}: where GDP growth came from, {START}-{END}",
                      xaxis_title="Year", yaxis_title="Percentage points", legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15))
    return fig

decomposition_figure()

Sources. Data: Penn World Table 11.0 (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015), rgdpna, rnna and emp. Prepared file: data/appD/pwt_accounting.csv (see the data notes). Method: the Growth Atlas. Chart: inspired by the growth accounting of Chapter 6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

Python note. barmode="relative" stacks positive bars upwards and negative bars downwards from zero, so a year with a negative contribution still reads correctly. legendgroup ties the bars of one kind together, which matters when the same legend serves several panels (Fig. 4).

What to notice.

  • In 2020 the pandemic cut U.S. employment, so the labour contribution fell to about −3.7 percentage points, while TFP rose. Workers who kept their jobs were, on average, more productive, and output per worker held up: a classic composition effect that the residual absorbs.
  • TFP contributions swing much more from year to year than capital contributions, because the capital stock changes slowly while output moves with the business cycle.

D.6 Growth accounting for your countries

Fig. 4: Contributions to GDP growth, economy by economy

Goal. Compare the growth accounting of several economies side by side, and test how it changes with the capital share \(\alpha\) and the measure of labour.

Some economies lack hours or human capital in some years. A small helper writes their codes under the title, so a missing panel is never a mystery.

def no_data_note(codes, d):
    """A small second title line naming the chosen economies that have no data in d."""
    missing = []
    for code in codes:
        if code not in set(d["iso3"]):
            missing.append(code)
    if len(missing) == 0:
        return ""
    return "<br><sup>No data: " + ", ".join(missing) + "</sup>"
def growth_panels(codes=tuple(COUNTRIES), alpha=ALPHA, labour="persons"):
    """Fig. 4: one growth accounting panel per chosen economy, equation (2)."""
    d = growth_accounting(alpha, labour)
    codes = list(codes)[:9]                         # at most nine panels
    if len(codes) == 0:
        codes = ["USA"]                             # nothing chosen: show the United States
    rows = (len(codes) + 2) // 3
    titles = []
    for code in codes:
        titles.append(NAMES[code][:28])
    fig = make_subplots(rows=rows, cols=3, shared_yaxes=True, vertical_spacing=0.12, subplot_titles=titles)
    for i, code in enumerate(codes):
        add_decomposition(fig, d[d["iso3"] == code], row=i // 3 + 1, col=i % 3 + 1, legend=(i == 0))
    note = no_data_note(codes, d)
    fig.update_layout(barmode="relative", height=300 + 260 * rows, legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.08),
                      title=f"Contributions to GDP growth, α = {alpha:.2f}, labour = {LABOUR[labour]}{note}")
    shown = d[d["iso3"].isin(codes)][["gdp", "capital", "labour", "tfp"]]
    if shown.abs().max().max() < 20:                # one fixed scale, unless a year is far outside it
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[-20, 20])
    return fig

What to notice.

  • China grew fastest, and both capital and TFP contributed a lot. Its capital contribution stayed above 2 percentage points in almost every year.
  • India and Nigeria had large labour contributions: their working-age populations grew fast.
  • Mexico’s growth came almost entirely from adding capital and workers; its average TFP contribution was slightly negative.
  • Raising \(\alpha\) moves growth from labour to capital in economies whose capital grew faster than labour (China, Korea), and lowers their TFP. Switching from persons to hours lowers the labour contribution where hours per worker fell (Korea), and moves that growth into TFP.

D.7 Averages over periods and decades

Yearly numbers are noisy. Over longer periods, business-cycle swings cancel out and the residual reflects long-run productivity growth more closely.

Fig. 5: Average contributions over a period

Goal. Compare average contributions across your economies over a period you choose.

def period_averages(codes=tuple(COUNTRIES), start=START, end=END, alpha=ALPHA, labour="persons"):
    """Average contributions to GDP growth over start-end, one row per economy."""
    d = growth_accounting(alpha, labour)
    d = d[d["iso3"].isin(codes) & (d["year"] >= start) & (d["year"] <= end)]
    return d.groupby("country")[["gdp", "capital", "labour", "tfp"]].mean().sort_values("gdp")

def average_figure(codes=tuple(COUNTRIES), start=START, end=END, alpha=ALPHA, labour="persons"):
    """Fig. 5: stacked average contributions, with average GDP growth as a diamond."""
    avg = period_averages(codes, start, end, alpha, labour).reset_index()
    avg["gdp"] = avg["gdp"].round(4)
    fig = go.Figure()
    for column, label, color in PARTS:
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=avg["country"], y=avg[column], name=label, marker_color=color))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=avg["country"], y=avg["gdp"], mode="markers", name="GDP growth, g_Y",
                             marker=dict(color="black", symbol="diamond", size=12)))
    fig.update_layout(barmode="relative", title=f"Average contributions to GDP growth, {start}-{end}",
                      yaxis_title="Percentage points a year")
    parts = avg[["capital", "labour", "tfp"]]
    if parts.clip(lower=0).sum(axis=1).max() < 12 and parts.clip(upper=0).sum(axis=1).min() > -4:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[-4, 12])            # one fixed scale, so periods are easy to compare
    return fig

D.8 Development accounting: the theory

Growth accounting compares an economy with its own past. Development accounting compares economies with each other in one year. Chapter 4 did a first version: with output per person \(y = \bar{A} k^{1/3}\), it found that differences in capital per person explain little of the income gap between rich and poor economies, and TFP explains most of it. We now add human capital, and write the equation in a form that avoids crediting capital for what TFP achieved.

Assumptions

  1. Output is produced with physical capital \(K\) and human capital \(H = hL\): \(L\) workers, each with \(h\) units of skills from schooling (PWT’s hc index), \[Y = A K^{\alpha} (hL)^{1-\alpha} . \tag{4}\]
  2. The capital share is \(\alpha = 0.33\) in every economy, as in Hall and Jones (1999) and Caunedo’s code.
  3. Output and capital are measured at PPPs, so they are comparable across economies: output per worker \(y = Y/L\) is rgdpo / emp, and the capital–output ratio \(K/Y\) is cn / cgdpo.

Deriving the equation

Divide equation (4) by \(L\). With \(k = K/L\), output per worker is

\[ y = A k^{\alpha} h^{1-\alpha} . \]

This is the form of Chapter 4, with schooling added. But \(k\) is not independent of \(A\): an economy with a higher TFP produces more, saves more and builds a larger capital stock (Chapter 5). Part of its high \(k\) is therefore caused by TFP. To avoid crediting capital for it, write capital per worker as the capital–output ratio times output per worker, \(k = (K/Y)\, y\):

\[ y = A \left(\frac{K}{Y}\right)^{\alpha} y^{\alpha} h^{1-\alpha} . \]

Divide both sides by \(y^{\alpha}\), so the left side becomes \(y^{1-\alpha}\):

\[ y^{1-\alpha} = A \left(\frac{K}{Y}\right)^{\alpha} h^{1-\alpha} . \]

Raise both sides to the power \(1/(1-\alpha)\):

\[ y = \underbrace{A^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}}_{\text{TFP term}} \;\times\; \underbrace{\left(\frac{K}{Y}\right)^{\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}}}_{\text{capital term}} \;\times\; \underbrace{h}_{\text{human capital}} . \tag{5} \]

Output per worker is the product of three terms. In the Solow model the capital–output ratio is \(s/(n+\bar{d})\) in steady state, which does not depend on \(A\), so the capital term measures the part of capital that is not driven by TFP. Hall and Jones (1999) and Caselli (2005) discuss this choice.

The residual and the comparison with the United States

As in growth accounting, the TFP term is the residual: what is left of \(y\) after the measured inputs,

\[ A^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}} = \frac{y}{(K/Y)^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)}\; h} . \tag{6} \]

Divide equation (5) for economy \(i\) by the same equation for the United States. Each term becomes a ratio, and a value of 0.5 means “half the U.S. level”:

\[ \frac{y_i}{y_{US}} = \frac{A_i^{1/(1-\alpha)}}{A_{US}^{1/(1-\alpha)}} \times \frac{(K/Y)_i^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)}}{(K/Y)_{US}^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)}} \times \frac{h_i}{h_{US}} . \tag{7} \]

Splitting the gap

Turn each ratio upside down to get the gap factors: \(T_i\) for TFP, \(K_i\) for the capital term and \(H_i\) for human capital, each equal to the U.S. level divided by economy \(i\)’s level. The income gap is their product, \(y_{US}/y_i = T_i \times K_i \times H_i\). Caunedo’s code compares the TFP gap with the gap that the two inputs create together, \(K_i \times H_i\), and splits the rest between the two inputs in proportion to their gap factors:

\[ s^{TFP}_i = \frac{T_i}{T_i + K_i H_i}, \qquad s^{K}_i = \frac{K_i}{K_i + H_i}\,(1 - s^{TFP}_i), \qquad s^{H}_i = \frac{H_i}{K_i + H_i}\,(1 - s^{TFP}_i) . \tag{8} \]

The three shares add up to one. If TFP and the inputs open gaps of the same size (\(T_i = K_i H_i\)), the TFP share is one half; if the TFP gap is three times the input gap, it is three quarters.

Intuition. Development accounting asks: if this economy had U.S. levels of capital (relative to output) and of schooling, how much richer would it be? The TFP term answers what is left: how much it would still lag behind.

D.9 Development accounting for your countries

Goal. Compute equations (5) to (8) for every economy in one year, with labour measured per worker (the default) or per hour.

The function keeps one year, computes the three terms of equation (5), divides by the U.S. values, and adds the shares of equation (8). It drops Venezuela, whose PWT output after 2017 is not plausible (hyperinflation broke its price data), as in the chapters.

def dev_levels(year=2023, per="worker", alpha=ALPHA):
    """Equations (5) and (6): output per worker, the capital term, human capital and TFP, in one year."""
    d = pwt[(pwt["year"] == year) & (pwt["iso3"] != "VEN")].copy()
    d["workers"] = d["emp"]
    if per == "hour":
        d["workers"] = d["emp"] * d["avh"]          # output per hour instead of per worker
    d["y"] = d["rgdpo"] / d["workers"]
    d["ky"] = (d["cn"] / d["cgdpo"]) ** (alpha / (1 - alpha))
    d["h"] = d["hc"]
    d["tfp"] = d["y"] / (d["ky"] * d["h"])
    return d.dropna(subset=["y", "ky", "h", "tfp"])
def relative_to_us(d):
    """Equations (7) and (8): each term relative to the United States, and the shares of the gap."""
    d = d.copy()
    us = d[d["iso3"] == "USA"].iloc[0]
    for col in ["y", "ky", "h", "tfp"]:
        d[col + "_rel"] = d[col] / us[col]
    T, K, H = 1 / d["tfp_rel"], 1 / d["ky_rel"], 1 / d["h_rel"]
    d["share_tfp"] = T / (T + K * H)
    d["share_k"] = K / (K + H) * (1 - d["share_tfp"])
    d["share_h"] = H / (K + H) * (1 - d["share_tfp"])
    d.loc[d["iso3"] == "USA", ["share_tfp", "share_k", "share_h"]] = np.nan   # no gap with itself
    return d

def dev_accounting(year=2023, per="worker", alpha=ALPHA):
    """Development accounting in one year: levels, ratios to the United States and shares."""
    return relative_to_us(dev_levels(year, per, alpha))

da = dev_accounting()
print(len(da), "economies in 2023")

TERMS = [("y_rel", "Output per worker, y", "black"), ("ky_rel", "Capital term, (K/Y)^(α/(1−α))", BLUE),

def terms_figure(codes=tuple(COUNTRIES), year=2023, per="worker"):
    """Fig. 6: the terms of equation (7) for the chosen economies, United States = 1."""
    d = dev_accounting(year, per)

    if d[["y_rel", "ky_rel", "h_rel", "tfp_rel"]].max().max() < 2.4:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 2.4])            # one fixed scale, unless an economy is far above it
    return fig

fig = slider_figure(terms_figure, "year", [1990, 2000, 2010, 2023], start=2023, label="year")

Sources. Data: Penn World Table 11.0 (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015), rgdpo, cgdpo, cn, emp, avh and hc. Prepared file: data/appD/pwt_accounting.csv (see the data notes). Method: Caunedo, STEG Lecture 2. Chart: inspired by the development accounting of Chapter 4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The capital term is close to 1, or above it, in every one of the default economies: poorer economies do not have lower capital–output ratios. Capital per worker is low in Nigeria because output per worker is low, not the other way round.
  • Human capital in India and Nigeria is about 55 to 60 percent of the U.S. level: schooling explains part of the gap.
  • The TFP term is the furthest from 1. Nigeria’s is about 9 percent of the U.S. level, India’s about 19 percent. Most of the income gap is a TFP gap.

Fig. 7: How much of the gap is due to TFP?

Goal. Look at all economies at once: plot the TFP share of each economy’s gap, equation (8), against its output per worker.

def share_scatter(codes=tuple(COUNTRIES), year=2023):
    """Fig. 7: the TFP share of the income gap against output per worker, all economies."""
    d = dev_accounting(year).dropna(subset=["share_tfp"])
    d["group"] = np.where(d["iso3"].isin(codes), "Your economies", "Other economies")
    d["label"] = np.where(d["iso3"].isin(codes), d["iso3"], "")
    fig = px.scatter(d, x="y_rel", y="share_tfp", color="group", text="label", hover_name="country",
                     log_x=True, range_x=[0.008, 12], range_y=[0, 1.05],
                     color_discrete_map={"Your economies": RUST, "Other economies": BLUE},
                     labels={"y_rel": "Output per worker (United States = 1, ratio scale)",
                             "share_tfp": "Share of the gap due to TFP", "group": ""},
                     title=f"In {year}, the poorer the economy, the larger the share of its gap due to TFP")
    fig.update_traces(textposition="top center")
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=[0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10])
    return fig

share_scatter()
interact(share_scatter, codes=country_picker(COUNTRIES),
         year=IntSlider(value=2023, min=1970, max=2023, description="year", style=WIDE));

What to notice.

  • In the 31 poorest economies, with less than a tenth of U.S. output per worker, TFP accounts for 70 to 90 percent of the gap in most cases (the median is about 80 percent).
  • Economies richer than the United States (Ireland, Norway, Switzerland, Singapore, Qatar, Brunei) appear on the right of 1. Their “gaps” are negative, and the shares measure how much each term contributes to their lead.
  • Press play on the website: the cloud drifts up over time. TFP explains a larger share of income gaps in 2023 than in 1990, as Fig. 8 shows more clearly.

Your turn. Compute the TFP share of the gap for Korea per worker and per hour in 2023. Why do they differ?

Show the answer 
for per in ["worker", "hour"]:
    d = dev_accounting(2023, per)
    korea = d[d["iso3"] == "KOR"].iloc[0]
    print(per, round(korea["y_rel"], 3), round(korea["share_tfp"], 3))

Koreans work more hours a year than Americans, so Korea is further behind in output per hour than in output per worker. Its TFP gap, and the TFP share, are larger per hour.

D.10 How much do inputs explain?

Equation (8) gives a share for each economy. Two summary measures describe all economies together.

Fig. 8: The median shares over time

def medians_figure(codes=tuple(COUNTRIES)):
    """Fig. 8: median shares of the income gap, and the TFP share of the chosen economies."""
    fig = go.Figure()
    for column, color in [("TFP", RUST), ("Physical capital", BLUE), ("Human capital", TEAL)]:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=medians["year"], y=medians[column], mode="lines",
                                 name=f"Median share: {column}", line=dict(color=color, width=3)))
    for code in codes:
        if code == "USA":
            continue                                   # the United States has no gap with itself
        path = []
        for year in medians["year"]:
            row = DA_PANEL[(DA_PANEL["iso3"] == code) & (DA_PANEL["year"] == year)]
            path.append(row["share_tfp"].iloc[0] if len(row) else None)
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=medians["year"], y=path, mode="lines",
                                 line=dict(dash="dot", width=1.5, color=country_colors(codes)[NAMES[code]]),
                                 name=f"TFP share: {NAMES[code][:24]}"))
    fig.update_layout(title="TFP explains a growing share of income gaps", xaxis_title="Year",
                      yaxis=dict(title="Share of the gap with the United States", range=[0, 1]))
    return fig

The function reads the TFP shares of every economy and year from one panel, DA_PANEL, which we build once with pd.concat:

frames = []
for year in range(1970, 2024):
    frames.append(dev_accounting(year)[["iso3", "year", "share_tfp"]])
DA_PANEL = pd.concat(frames)
medians_figure()

Sources. Data: Penn World Table 11.0 (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015). Prepared file: data/appD/pwt_accounting.csv (see the data notes). Method and chart: inspired by Caunedo, STEG Lecture 2, and by the development accounting of Chapter 4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The median TFP share rose from about 0.44 in 1970 to about 0.71 in 2023. The shares of physical and human capital fell. Part of this comes from the sample: 107 economies have data in 1970, and 142 from 1990 on. But the rise continues after 1990, when the sample is fixed.
  • Schooling has spread to poor economies faster than income has: their human capital gaps narrowed, so a larger part of the remaining gap is a TFP gap.

The success of factor-only models

Caselli (2005) asks a different question: if all economies had the same TFP, how much of the dispersion of income across economies would remain? Write \(y^{KH}_i = (K/Y)_i^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)} h_i\) for the part of output per worker explained by the inputs in equation (5). The success of this factor-only model is the ratio of the variances of the logs:

\[ \text{success} = \frac{\operatorname{var}\left[\ln y^{KH}\right]}{\operatorname{var}\left[\ln y\right]} . \tag{9} \]

A success of 1 means inputs explain all of the differences in income; a success of 0 means they explain none. Caunedo’s code also reports the success of each input on its own.

def success(d):
    """Equation (9): the share of the variance of log output per worker explained by the inputs."""
    var_y = np.log(d["y"]).var()
    return {"economies": len(d),
            "inputs": np.log(d["ky"] * d["h"]).var() / var_y,
            "physical capital": np.log(d["ky"]).var() / var_y,
            "human capital": np.log(d["h"]).var() / var_y}

result = success(dev_levels(2023))
for key, value in result.items():
    print(f"{key:>17}: {value:.3f}")
        economies: 143.000
           inputs: 0.157
 physical capital: 0.053
    human capital: 0.068

What to notice. Inputs explain only about 16 percent of the variance of log output per worker across 143 economies in 2023. The other 84 percent is TFP.

This is lower than the success of about 0.3 to 0.4 that Caselli (2005) reports with the form of Chapter 4, \(y^{KH} = k^{\alpha} h^{1-\alpha}\). That form credits physical capital for the capital that TFP itself induces, as we discussed in Section D.8. We can compute it with our data too:

d = dev_levels(2023)
k = d["cn"] / d["workers"]                          # capital per worker, current PPPs
y_kh = k ** ALPHA * d["h"] ** (1 - ALPHA)
print(f"Success with capital per worker (Chapter 4 form): {np.log(y_kh).var() / np.log(d['y']).var():.3f}")
Success with capital per worker (Chapter 4 form): 0.301

The same data give a success of about 0.30 in the capital-per-worker form, twice the 0.16 of the capital–output form. How much “inputs” explain depends on whether capital that TFP induces is counted as capital or as TFP.

Your turn. Compute the success of the inputs in 1990 and in 2010. Has it changed?

Show the answer 
for year in [1990, 2010, 2023]:
    print(year, round(success(dev_levels(year))["inputs"], 3))

The success of the inputs fell from about 0.21 in 1990 to about 0.14 in 2010, and was about 0.16 in 2023. Inputs explain less of the spread of incomes than they did in 1990, which agrees with the rising TFP share of Fig. 8. The two measures still answer different questions: Fig. 8 looks at the typical economy’s gap with the United States, the success measure at the spread of all economies.

D.11 Robustness: hours, labour shares and natural resources

Every accounting exercise rests on choices. Caunedo’s code tests three of them, and so do we.

  1. Per hour instead of per worker. Caunedo measures output per hour, \(Y/(L \times \text{hours})\). Hours exist for fewer economies, which is why our default is per worker.
  2. Country labour shares instead of a common \(\alpha\). PWT’s labsh is the share of labour income in GDP in each economy and year. Using it, the capital term becomes \((K/Y)^{(1-\text{labsh})/\text{labsh}}\).
  3. GDP net of natural-resource rents. Part of GDP in oil and mining economies is a rent on a natural resource, not the product of reproducible capital, labour and TFP. Caunedo removes these rents, using the World Bank’s total natural resource rents as a percent of GDP: \(Y^{net} = Y \times (1 - \text{rents}/100)\), applied to both rgdpo and cgdpo. Like her, we then drop Ireland and Macao, whose GDP includes large foreign profits.

The data on rents come from the World Bank. They end in 2021, and the data script carries each economy’s last value forward to 2023.

rents = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "nat_res_rents.csv")
top = rents[rents["year"] == 2021].nlargest(5, "rents_pct")
top["country"] = top["iso3"].map(NAMES)
print(rents.shape[0], "rows. The largest rents in 2021, in percent of GDP:")
top[["country", "rents_pct"]]
8512 rows. The largest rents in 2021, in percent of GDP:
country rents_pct
3900 Iraq 43.4459
1759 D.R. of the Congo 38.8273
1813 Congo 37.7125
8455 Zambia 35.2641
3412 Guyana 33.6833

Each variant changes one step of dev_levels. Rather than write three new functions, we write one that takes the variant’s name and changes the data before calling the same formulas.

def dev_variant(year=2023, variant="per worker"):
    """Development accounting levels, equations (5) and (6), under one of four variants."""
    if variant == "per hour":
        return dev_levels(year, per="hour")
    d = dev_levels(year)
    if variant == "labour shares":
        d["ky"] = (d["cn"] / d["cgdpo"]) ** ((1 - d["labsh"]) / d["labsh"])
    if variant == "net of rents":
        d = d.merge(rents[rents["year"] == year][["iso3", "rents_pct"]], on="iso3")
        d = d[~d["iso3"].isin(["IRL", "MAC"])]
        d["y"] = d["y"] * (1 - d["rents_pct"] / 100)
        d["ky"] = (d["cn"] / (d["cgdpo"] * (1 - d["rents_pct"] / 100))) ** (ALPHA / (1 - ALPHA))
    d["tfp"] = d["y"] / (d["ky"] * d["h"])
    return d.dropna(subset=["y", "ky", "h", "tfp"])

VARIANTS = ["per worker", "per hour", "labour shares", "net of rents"]

A first look at the labour shares. Before using them, sort them and look at the extremes:

shares_2023 = pwt[pwt["year"] == 2023][["country", "labsh"]].dropna().sort_values("labsh")
print(shares_2023.head(5).to_string(index=False))
print("Median labour share:", round(shares_2023["labsh"].median(), 3))
                           country    labsh
Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) 0.084364
          Central African Republic 0.164320
                             Qatar 0.176720
                            Angola 0.223240
                            Kuwait 0.249490
Median labour share: 0.52

The median labour share is about 0.52, so the median capital share is about 0.48, well above our 0.33. And in oil economies such as Qatar the labour share is below 0.2, because the oil rent is counted as capital income. With labsh = 0.18, the exponent of the capital term is \((1-0.18)/0.18 \approx 4.6\) instead of 0.49, so small differences in \(K/Y\) become huge differences in the capital term.

The four variants side by side

rows = []
for variant in VARIANTS:
    d = relative_to_us(dev_variant(2023, variant))
    s = success(d)
    rows.append({"variant": variant, "economies": s["economies"], "success of inputs": s["inputs"],
                 "median TFP share": d["share_tfp"].median()})
robust = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("variant")
robust.round(3)
economies success of inputs median TFP share
variant
per worker 143 0.157 0.706
per hour 119 0.151 0.713
labour shares 119 1.944 0.846
net of rents 140 0.150 0.734

What to notice.

  • Per hour and net of rents give almost the same answers as the baseline: inputs explain about 15 percent of the variance, and the median TFP share is about 0.7.
  • Country labour shares give a success far above 1, which is impossible for a share of the variance. The huge exponents of the oil economies blow up the variance of the capital term. This is why development accounting usually keeps one common \(\alpha\), as Hall and Jones (1999), Caselli (2005) and Caunedo do. Gollin (2002) shows that once the income of the self-employed is counted as labour income, labour shares are much more similar across economies.

Fig. 9: The median TFP share under each variant

Your turn. How does removing natural-resource rents change Nigeria’s numbers in 2023? Compare its output per worker relative to the United States and its TFP share with and without the adjustment.

Show the answer 
for variant in ["per worker", "net of rents"]:
    d = relative_to_us(dev_variant(2023, variant))
    nigeria = d[d["iso3"] == "NGA"].iloc[0]

Nigeria’s oil rents are a sizeable share of its GDP. Removing them lowers its output per worker relative to the United States, and with it the TFP term, so its TFP share rises slightly.

# Your turn: try it here

D.12 Go further

  • Capital services instead of stocks. PWT also provides ck and rkna, capital services, which weight each type of asset (computers, buildings, machines) by its rental price. Caunedo’s code includes this variant, commented out.
  • PWT’s own TFP. PWT publishes ctfp (TFP levels relative to the United States) and rtfpna (TFP growth), computed with country labour shares and capital services. Comparing them with our residuals shows how much the method matters.
  • Better human capital. The hc index counts years of schooling, not what students learn or the skills they bring to work. Hendricks and Schoellman (2023) measure skills with the wage gains of migrants and find a larger role for human capital.
  • Regions. The Growth Atlas also aggregates economies into regions, weighting each economy’s growth by its GDP. Try it with groupby("region") and a weighted average.

Common errors and how to fix them

Error or symptom What it usually means What to do
KeyError: 'XYZ' a country code that is not in PWT print NAMES and copy the exact three-letter code
a panel is missing in Fig. 4 the economy lacks hours or human capital for the chosen labour measure switch the labour measure back to persons engaged
IndexError: single positional indexer is out-of-bounds the United States has no data in that year or variant choose a year with U.S. data; every year from 1970 works
a growth rate of hundreds of percent a break in a series (a war, a new country, a currency reform) look at the levels with pwt[pwt["iso3"] == code]
shares above 1 or below 0 an economy richer than the United States, or labour shares near 0 read Section D.11 before interpreting them
Venezuela looks a hundred times poorer than its neighbours PWT prices broke during hyperinflation the notebook drops Venezuela from development accounting

Concluding remarks

  • The Penn World Table provides comparable output and inputs for 185 economies. Use national-price series (rgdpna, rnna) for growth over time and PPP series (rgdpo, cgdpo, cn) for levels across economies.
  • Growth accounting, equation (2), splits GDP growth into the contributions of capital, labour and TFP, with TFP as the residual of equation (3). Since 1990, TFP explains more than half of China’s growth, close to half of U.S. growth, and nothing of Mexico’s.
  • Development accounting, equation (5), writes output per worker as a TFP term, a capital–output term and human capital. Relative to the United States, the capital term is close to 1 almost everywhere, and the TFP term carries most of the gap: the median TFP share of the gap in equation (8) is about 0.7 in 2023.
  • The success of inputs, equation (9), is only about 0.15 in the capital–output form and about 0.3 in the capital-per-worker form. Most of the differences in income across economies are differences in TFP, a result that holds per hour and net of natural-resource rents.
  • Accounting says where the differences are, not why. The models of Chapters 5 and 6 explain how investment, population growth and ideas shape capital and TFP.
